title: Matthew 2:16–18
context: When Herod realizes the Magi will not return, he erupts in rage and slaughters the boys of Bethlehem; Matthew frames the horror with Jeremiah’s lament of Rachel weeping for her children.

voices.heading: Voices from both camps
voices.intro: Historic words on he erupts in rage and slaughters the boys of Bethlehem; Matthew frames the horror with Jeremiah’s lament of Rachel—so each camp speaks in its own voice beside Matthew 2:16–18.
voices.note: Quotations lightly abridged for length; wording follows standard English translations of the sources named.

arminian.quote: Then Herod, seeing that he was deluded by the wise men - So did his pride teach him to regard this action, as if it were intended to expose him to the derision of his subjects. Sending forth - a party of soldiers: In all the confines thereof - In all the neighbouring places, of which Rama was one.
arminian.source: Explanatory Notes upon the New Testament (on Matt 2:16–18)

reformed.quote: And when they had departed How many days elapsed from the departure of the Magi, till Joseph was ordered to flee into Egypt, is not known, nor is it of much importance to inquire: only it is probable that the Lord spared Mary, till she was so far recovered from childbirth as to be able to perform the journey. It was a wonderful purpose of God, that he chose to preserve his Son by flight.
reformed.source: Commentary on a Harmony of the Evangelists (on Matt 2:16–18)

verses.text: Then Herod, when he saw that he had been tricked by the wise men, became furious, and he sent and killed all the male children in Bethlehem and in all that region who were two years old or under, according to the time that he had ascertained from the wise men.
verses.arminianNotes:
Matthew refuses to soften tyranny. Herod’s fury becomes policy: children die because a king will not yield the throne to God’s Christ.

Classical Arminians insist God is not the author of this evil. Human agents freely choose massacre; the gospel still names the crime. Grief and moral clarity belong together under a God who hates injustice and invites the world to the true King.
verses.reformedNotes:
The slaughter is wholly Herod’s wickedness—and it occurs within a providence that has already relocated the Messiah. God restrains evil from destroying the Son without making Herod’s sin His own doing.

Reformed pastoral hold: sovereignty is not a shrug over corpses. It is the assurance that tyrants do not finally write history, while their guilt remains undiluted.
verses.keyContrast: Both refuse to blame God for Herod’s murder. Arminians typically stress creaturely freedom and God’s non-causation of sin; Reformed theology typically stresses meticulous providence that limits evil’s reach to the Christ-child while never making God the author of Herod’s rage.

verses.text: Then was fulfilled what was spoken by the prophet Jeremiah:
verses.arminianNotes:
Fulfillment language here is lament, not celebration. Scripture gives words for tears when the powerful crush the weak.

Shared pastoral gift: God does not gaslight the suffering. He speaks through Jeremiah so the church can weep truthfully and still hope.
verses.reformedNotes:
Even atrocity sits inside a canonical frame Matthew recognizes. “Fulfilled” does not mean God delighted in the killing; it means the pattern of Israel’s sorrow finds a terrible echo in Messiah’s infancy.

God’s Word interprets history without excusing its villains.

verses.text:
“A voice was heard in Ramah,
weeping and loud lamentation,
Rachel weeping for her children;
she refused to be comforted, because they are no more.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Rachel’s voice refuses cheap comfort. Matthew honors mothers who will not pretend the loss is small. The incarnation enters a world of real blood and real cries.

Arminian hope does not silence lament: the same God who draws near in Christ will one day wipe tears—and until then, the church may weep with those who weep while pointing to the surviving King.
verses.reformedNotes:
Jeremiah 31 holds both exile’s grief and the promise of new covenant hope beyond it. Matthew cites the grief now; the wider chapter’s consolation still belongs to God’s people in Christ.

Reformed comfort in darkness: Rachel’s tears are heard, and they are not the last word in the story God is writing through His Son.
